title: Revelation 16:12–21
context: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates for the kings from the east, and demonic spirits gather the kings of the world for battle at Armageddon. Christ warns that he comes like a thief. The seventh bowl brings a voice declaring “It is done,” a great earthquake, the fall of Babylon, and huge hailstones, yet people still curse God.

verses.text: The sixth poured out his bowl on the great river, the Euphrates. Its water was dried up, that the way might be prepared for the kings that come from the sunrise.
verses.arminianNotes: The Euphrates dries up for the kings from the east. Interpreters link this to Parthian invaders, to future armies, or to a symbol of the world’s powers gathering against God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers usually read the imagery symbolically.

verses.text: I saw coming out of the mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits, something like frogs;
verses.arminianNotes: Frog-like unclean spirits come from the dragon, beast, and false prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see deception at the root of the world’s opposition.

verses.text: for they are spirits of demons, performing signs, which go out to the kings of the whole inhabited earth, to gather them together for the war of that great day of God the Almighty.
verses.arminianNotes: Demonic spirits gather the kings for the war of the great day of God the Almighty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God permitting even the gathering of his enemies for their defeat.

verses.text: “Behold, I come like a thief. Blessed is he who watches, and keeps his clothes, so that he doesn’t walk naked, and they see his shame.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I come like a thief. Blessed is he who watches.” Arminian readers see a call to watchfulness that applies to all believers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see watchfulness as the mark of those who belong to Christ.

verses.text: He gathered them together into the place which is called in Hebrew, “Harmagedon”.
verses.arminianNotes: Harmagedon is often linked with Megiddo, the site of famous battles. Futurists often expect a literal battle there, while others see a symbol of the final conflict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers usually see the final defeat of God’s enemies rather than a geographic forecast.

verses.text: The seventh poured out his bowl into the air. A loud voice came out of the temple of heaven, from the throne, saying, “It is done!”
verses.arminianNotes: The seventh bowl brings a voice from the throne: “It is done!”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s purpose accomplished.

verses.text: There were lightnings, sounds, and thunders; and there was a great earthquake such as has not happened since there were men on the earth—so great an earthquake and so mighty.
verses.arminianNotes: The greatest earthquake in history follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shaking of all things before the end.

verses.text: The great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell. Babylon the great was remembered in the sight of God, to give to her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath.
verses.arminianNotes: Babylon is split, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembers Babylon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the judgment of the world system.

verses.text: Every island fled away, and the mountains were not found.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the end of the present order.

verses.text: Great hailstones, about the weight of a talent, came down out of the sky on people. People blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, for this plague was exceedingly severe.
verses.arminianNotes: Huge hailstones fall, and people curse God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see rebellion persisting to the end.
